skill.name: Cut the sentence that doesn't belong
skill.why: One stray sentence pulls readers off track. Cut it and the paragraph stays clear.
skill.how: Find what the paragraph is about. Check each sentence. Cut the one that wanders off.

steps.say: First I work out what the whole paragraph is about. Read every sentence.

show.text: Their claws rip through hard dirt.
They can dig a tunnel in one night.

options.text: what wombats eat
options.reason: Nothing here is about food. What does every sentence talk about?

options.text: how wombats dig
wombats' claws
options.reason: Claws are in one sentence. What do all three sentences talk about?

steps.win: Yes! It's all about digging. That's the main idea. The first sentence often says it.

steps.say: A first sentence that tells the main idea is called a topic sentence. Now check the rest.

show.nudge: That one tells the main idea. Check the others against it.
Claws that rip dirt are about digging. It belongs.

show.text: Mo's lunch box has a wombat.
They dig a tunnel in a night.
show.nudge: A tunnel in one night shows how well they dig. It belongs.

steps.ask: Tap the sentence that isn't about digging.
steps.win: Yes! Mo's lunch box isn't about digging. It wanders off, so cut it.

steps.say: Here is a sneaky one. Every sentence is about wombats. Check each one against the main idea.

show.nudge: That one tells the main idea. Check the others against it.
Claws that rip dirt are about digging. It belongs.

show.text: Wombats live for about fifteen years.
Their tunnels can be thirty metres long.
show.nudge: Long tunnels show how much they dig. It belongs.

steps.ask: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong.
steps.win: Yes! It's about wombats, but not about digging. The same animal isn't enough.

steps.say: Zed says, 'Cut anything someone thinks or says.' Let's test that on Gus's paragraph.

show.nudge: That one tells the main idea. Check the others against it.
That shows how far it stretches. It belongs.

show.text: Mo says it stretches like pizza cheese.
show.nudge: Mo's words are about the stretch, so they belong. Which sentence isn't?

steps.ask: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong.
steps.win: Yes! Green socks have nothing to do with stretchy slime. What Mo says is about the slime, so it stays.

steps.say: After a cut, you can add a sentence that fits. Back to the wombats.
steps.ask: Which sentence belongs in the digging paragraph?

options.text: Wombats sleep all day.
options.reason: That's about wombats, but is it about digging?

options.text: Baby wombats ride in a pouch.
options.reason: Still wombats, but not digging. Check it against the main idea.

options.text: Their back feet kick the dirt away.

steps.win: Yes! Kicking dirt away is part of digging. Every sentence now sticks to the main idea.

terms.means: What the whole paragraph is about. The first sentence often says it.
Not about the main idea, even if it's the same animal or person.
Sticks to the main idea. Someone's opinion can belong too.

examples.text: Mo says it stretches like cheese.

card.test: Find the main idea. Check each sentence against it. Cut the one that wanders off.

weDo.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong in a paragraph about Mo's terrible cooking.
weDo.hint: What is the paragraph about? Which sentence talks about something else?
weDo.success: The paragraph is about Mo's terrible cooking. His favourite colour has nothing to do with it.

parts.tap: Mo is the worst cook on the Soggy Biscuit.
parts.reason: This is the first sentence, which says what the paragraph is about.

parts.tap: His fish-finger custard made Gus turn green.
parts.reason: This belongs. It's an example of Mo's terrible cooking.

parts.tap: Mo's favourite colour is orange.
Even the seagulls won't eat his leftovers.
parts.reason: This belongs. It shows how bad his cooking is.

weDo.text: Tully loves the Reef Rays. She goes to every home game. She knows every player's number. She has a pet goldfish called Bubbles. Her bedroom walls are covered in Reef Rays posters.
weDo.hint: The paragraph is about Tully loving the Reef Rays. Which sentence isn't?
weDo.success: The paragraph is about Tully loving the Reef Rays. Her goldfish has nothing to do with footy.

options.text: She knows every player's number.
options.reason: This belongs. It shows how much she loves the team.

options.text: She has a pet goldfish called Bubbles.
Her bedroom walls are covered in Reef Rays posters.
options.reason: This belongs. Team posters show how much she loves the Reef Rays.

write.ask: Read the paragraph. Cut the sentence that doesn't belong, then write one that does.
given: Biscuit the dog loves the beach.
He chases every wave that rolls in.
The beach car park closes at six.
checks: I cut the sentence that wanders off
My new sentence is about Biscuit loving the beach
It tells the reader something new
write.model: Biscuit the dog loves the beach. He chases every wave that rolls in. He even digs holes so he can lie in the cool, wet sand.

creature.name: Strandle
creature.blurb: A rock warbler that weaves its hanging nest inside the volcano's caves, one strand at a time. Slip in a strand that doesn't belong and it plucks it straight back out.

encounters.frame: Wren's koala paragraph is on the editing desk. The Strandle has spotted a stray strand.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong in Wren's paragraph about koalas sleeping.
encounters.success: The paragraph is about koalas sleeping. Wren thinking they're cute tells you nothing about sleep.

parts.tap: Koalas sleep for most of the day.
parts.reason: This is the first sentence. It says the paragraph is about sleep.

parts.tap: I think koalas are the cutest animals in the bush.
They can sleep for up to twenty hours.
parts.reason: This belongs. It tells you how long koalas sleep.

parts.tap: They wedge themselves into a fork in the tree so they don't fall.
parts.reason: This belongs. It tells you how koalas stay safe while they sleep.

parts.tap: A sleepy koala can doze through a thunderstorm.
parts.reason: This belongs. It shows how deeply koalas sleep.

encounters.prompt: Which sentence should Mo cut?
encounters.success: The paragraph is about Mo's terrible pancakes. His fruit salad is a different dish.

options.text: Last week, one stuck to the ceiling for two days.
options.reason: This belongs. A pancake on the ceiling is one of the wrong reasons.

options.text: The crew now hides when Mo gets out the frying pan.
options.reason: This belongs. It shows how bad the pancakes are.

options.text: Mo's fruit salad is actually quite good.

encounters.success: The paragraph is about Tully's lucky boots, and her special knot is part of the boot ritual.

parts.tap: Tully's footy boots are her lucky boots.
parts.reason: The first sentence says the paragraph is about her lucky boots.

parts.tap: She has worn them in every final.

She never washes them before a big game.

The canteen sells hot chips at every game.

encounters.prompt: Does each sentence belong in Wren's paragraph about how sea turtles live? Sort them.
encounters.success: Every sentence that stays tells you how sea turtles live. A toy turtle and Wren's ice cream don't.

items.text: Sea turtles can hold their breath for hours.

items.text: Gus has a toy turtle on his desk.

items.text: Their flippers work like paddles.
items.reason: This belongs. It tells you how sea turtles swim.

items.text: Mothers lay their eggs on sandy beaches.
items.reason: This belongs. It's about how sea turtles have their babies.

items.text: Wren's favourite ice cream is mango.
items.reason: This is about Wren, not about how sea turtles live.

items.text: Some turtles swim thousands of kilometres.
items.reason: This belongs. It tells you how far sea turtles travel.

encounters.frame: Zed's space report has a sentence that floated off. The Strandle is on it.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong in a paragraph about the Moon having no air.
encounters.success: The paragraph is about the Moon having no air. How it travels around Earth is a different topic.

parts.tap: There is no air on the Moon.
parts.reason: The first sentence says what the paragraph is about, and this is it.

parts.tap: Astronauts must wear space suits to breathe.
parts.reason: This belongs. They need suits because there's no air.

parts.tap: Without air, there is no wind.
parts.reason: This belongs. It tells you what having no air means.

parts.tap: Sound can't travel there, so the Moon is silent.
parts.reason: This belongs. Sound needs air to travel.

parts.tap: The Moon goes around Earth about once a month.

encounters.frame: Zed's game review is going in the Redpen Rumble. The Strandle found a stray strand.
encounters.text: Zed's new game is all about speed. You race a jet-powered snail around a volcano. Zed says it's the fastest game he has ever played. The snail's shell comes in ten different colours. If you slow down, the lava catches you. The fastest players finish the whole race in under a minute.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence should Zed cut from his paragraph about speed?
encounters.success: The paragraph is about speed. The shell's colours have nothing to do with how fast you go.

options.text: Zed says it's the fastest game he has ever played.
options.reason: This belongs. Zed's opinion is about how fast the game is.

options.text: The snail's shell comes in ten different colours.
If you slow down, the lava catches you.
options.reason: This belongs. It shows why speed matters in the game.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote a paragraph about his robot, Clunk. The Strandle thinks one strand is loose.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong in Gus's paragraph.
encounters.success: The paragraph is about Clunk being a terrible helper. Gus's other robot is a different topic.

parts.tap: Clunk is the worst helper Gus has ever built.
parts.reason: This opening sentence says the paragraph is about Clunk being a bad helper.

parts.tap: Last week, he glued Gus's hands to the workbench for three hours.
parts.reason: This belongs. It's an example of Clunk being a terrible helper.

parts.tap: He sorted the screws by colour instead of size, so nothing fitted.
parts.reason: This belongs. It's another example of Clunk getting a job wrong.

parts.tap: When Gus asked him to sweep the deck, he swept the toolbox into the sea.
parts.reason: This belongs. It shows Clunk ruining another job.

parts.tap: Gus is also building a robot dog that can fetch his slippers.

encounters.frame: Indi wrote about how she painted her mural. The Strandle wants one strand gone.
encounters.text: Indi's mural on the canteen wall took her a whole month to paint. Honestly, painting is the best thing about Indi's whole week. She started by sketching it in chalk. Then she painted the sky, the sea and finally sixty tiny fish. On the last day, she signed her name in the corner.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence should Indi cut?
encounters.success: The paragraph is about how Indi painted her mural. How much she loves painting isn't one of the steps.

options.text: She started by sketching it in chalk.
options.reason: This belongs. It's the first step in painting the mural.

options.text: Honestly, painting is the best thing about Indi's whole week.
On the last day, she signed her name in the corner.
options.reason: This belongs. Signing it is the last step in making the mural.

encounters.frame: Zed's article about the old lighthouse has one strand that doesn't fit.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong, then choose one that fits.
encounters.success: The paragraph is about the lighthouse being haunted. A sudden chill on the stairs is another spooky sign.

parts.tap: The old lighthouse on Redpen Point is said to be haunted.
parts.reason: This is the first sentence. It says the paragraph is about the haunting.

parts.tap: The keeper's cottage next door now sells ice creams all summer.
Since 1995, fishers have seen a light in the window, even though nobody lives there.
parts.reason: This belongs. A mystery light is a sign of a haunting.

parts.tap: Others have heard footsteps on the stairs at midnight.
parts.reason: This belongs. Midnight footsteps are another spooky sign.

parts.tap: One keeper's dog refuses to go past the front door.
parts.reason: This belongs. The dog seems scared of something in there.

options.text: The lighthouse is open to visitors on weekends.
options.reason: This is about opening times, not the haunting.

options.text: Its lamp can be seen from twenty kilometres away.
options.reason: This is about how far the real lamp shines, not the ghost.

options.text: Some visitors say the air turns icy as they climb the stairs.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing a paragraph about why snot is useful. The Strandle is holding its nose.
encounters.prompt: Does each sentence belong in Gus's paragraph? Sort them.
encounters.success: The sentences that stay explain what snot does for you. Gus's sneeze and his snot jar don't.

items.text: Snot traps dust before it can get into your lungs.
items.reason: This belongs. Trapping dust is one way snot is useful.

items.text: Gus keeps a jar of his own snot on his desk.
items.reason: This is about Gus's collection, not why snot is useful.

items.text: It catches germs and helps wash them out of your nose.
items.reason: This belongs. Catching germs is another way snot helps you.

items.text: Gus once sneezed so hard that he fell off his chair.
items.reason: This is a funny story about a sneeze, not about why snot is useful.

items.text: Snot stops the inside of your nose from drying out.
items.reason: This belongs. Keeping your nose from drying out is a job snot does.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote a paragraph about learning the drums. The Strandle hears one beat out of place.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong in Zed's paragraph.
encounters.success: The paragraph is about why drumming is hard. What's in a drum kit doesn't show that.

parts.tap: Learning the drums is much harder than it looks.
parts.reason: The first sentence says the paragraph is about drumming being hard.

parts.tap: A drum kit usually has five drums and two or three cymbals.
You have to keep a steady beat for the whole song.
parts.reason: This belongs. It's one thing that makes drumming hard.

parts.tap: Each hand and foot often plays a different rhythm at the same time.
parts.reason: This belongs. It's another reason drumming is hard.

parts.tap: One wrong hit and the whole band can lose its place.
parts.reason: This belongs. It shows how much a drummer has to get right.

parts.tap: It took Zed a whole year to play one song without stopping.
parts.reason: This belongs. It shows how long drumming takes to learn.

encounters.frame: Wren's paragraph about echidnas has a stray strand. The Strandle is tugging at it.
encounters.text: Echidnas are built for finding food. Their long snout can sniff out ants underground. Strong claws rip open termite nests. Then a long, sticky tongue slurps up the insects. A baby echidna is called a puggle.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence should Wren cut?
encounters.success: The paragraph is about how echidnas find food. What a baby is called doesn't fit.

options.text: Strong claws rip open termite nests.
options.reason: This belongs. Ripping open nests is how echidnas get at their food.

options.text: Then a long, sticky tongue slurps up the insects.
options.reason: This belongs. The tongue is how echidnas eat what they find.

options.text: A baby echidna is called a puggle.

encounters.frame: The Redpen Rumble is running a travel page about the hot springs. The Strandle found a strand from another nest.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong.
encounters.success: The paragraph is about why the springs are so popular. How they formed is a different topic.

parts.tap: The hot springs on Redpen Volcano are the island's most popular spot for visitors.
parts.reason: This opening sentence says the paragraph is about the springs being popular.

parts.tap: Every morning, more than two hundred tourists queue at sunrise to soak in the steaming pools.
parts.reason: This belongs. Queues at sunrise show how popular the springs are.

parts.tap: Some travel from the other side of the islands just for one dip.
parts.reason: This belongs. People travelling that far shows how popular the springs are.

parts.tap: On weekends, booking ahead is the only way to get a pool to yourself.
parts.reason: This belongs. Needing to book shows how busy the springs get.

parts.tap: The springs formed thousands of years ago, when the volcano's heat warmed water deep underground.

encounters.frame: Mo is writing up one of his recipes for the Redpen Rumble. The Strandle wants one strand out.
encounters.text: Mo mashes six bananas into a tin of tuna and spreads it in a pie dish. Next, he pours a layer of custard on top. The pie sells for four dollars a slice at the canteen. Then he sprinkles crushed salt-and-vinegar chips over the custard. Finally, he bakes it for an hour, until the custard turns brown.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence should Mo cut?
encounters.success: There's no topic sentence, but every other line is a step in making the pie. The price isn't a step.

options.text: Next, he pours a layer of custard on top.
options.reason: This belongs. Pouring on the custard is the second step.

options.text: The pie sells for four dollars a slice at the canteen.
Then he sprinkles crushed salt-and-vinegar chips over the custard.
options.reason: This belongs. The chips are the next step in making the pie.

options.text: Finally, he bakes it for an hour, until the custard turns brown.
options.reason: This belongs. Baking is the last step.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote a paragraph about platypuses. The Strandle wants a better strand in her nest.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong, then choose one that fits.
encounters.success: The paragraph is about how a platypus hunts with its eyes shut. A bill that finds hidden worms fits.

parts.tap: A platypus hunts with its eyes shut.
parts.reason: The first sentence says what the paragraph is about, and this is it.

parts.tap: When it dives, it closes its eyes, ears and nostrils.
parts.reason: This belongs. It shows the platypus can't see or hear underwater.

parts.tap: Instead, its bill senses the tiny electric signals given off by moving prey.
parts.reason: This belongs. It explains how the platypus finds food without looking.

parts.tap: It sweeps its bill from side to side along the creek bed, feeling for shrimp and worms.
parts.reason: This belongs. It shows the platypus feeling for food instead of looking.

parts.tap: Platypuses dig long burrows in the creek bank to sleep in.

options.text: A platypus mother keeps her eggs warm by curling around them.
options.reason: This is about eggs, not how a platypus hunts.

options.text: Its bill is so sensitive that it can find a worm hidden under a pebble.
Platypus fur is so thick that it stays dry underneath, even underwater.
options.reason: This is about its fur, not how a platypus finds food.

options.text: Males have a sharp spur on each back leg.
options.reason: This is about the spur on its leg, not how it finds food.

encounters.frame: Zed is writing about Mars. The Strandle is checking his notes against his first sentence.
encounters.text: Zed's first sentence: 'Living on Mars would be very hard work.'
encounters.prompt: Does each sentence belong in Zed's paragraph? Sort them.
encounters.success: The first sentence says living there is hard work. Sentences about that stay, even Gus's opinion.

items.text: Settlers would need to grow all their food in sealed greenhouses.
items.reason: This belongs. Growing every meal in a greenhouse is hard work.

items.text: Zed has had a huge poster of Mars above his bed since Year 2.
items.reason: This is about Zed's bedroom, not about living on Mars.

items.text: Gus reckons fixing the air machines would be the worst job of all.
items.reason: This belongs. It's what Gus thinks, but it's about the hard work.

items.text: Homes would need thick walls to block the Sun's harmful rays.
items.reason: This belongs. Building homes like that is hard work.

items.text: Mars was named after the Roman god of war.
items.reason: It's about Mars, but not about how hard living there would be.

items.text: Dust storms could cover the solar panels for months, so someone would have to clean them.
items.reason: This belongs. Cleaning the panels is more hard work.

items.text: Mars has two tiny moons that look like lumpy potatoes.
items.reason: It's a fact about Mars, but it isn't about the work of living there.

encounters.frame: Indi is writing about the choir's trip to the city. The Strandle found a loose strand.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong.
encounters.success: The paragraph lists the trip's disasters. How many singers the choir has isn't one of them.

parts.tap: The choir's trip to the city was one disaster after another.
parts.reason: This is the first sentence. It says the paragraph is about disasters.

parts.tap: The choir has forty singers, from Year 3 to Year 6.
The bus broke down an hour after it left school.

parts.tap: The new bus had air conditioning that blasted freezing air the whole way.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote a paragraph for the athletics newsletter. The Strandle wants one strand out.
encounters.text: Tully's training plan for the cross-country race starts six weeks out. In the first two weeks, she runs three kilometres every second day. Then she adds a hill run each Saturday. Tully says the hill runs build the strength she needs for the last climb. The race is held every year in the last week of term. In the final week, she rests more and only jogs. On race morning, she eats porridge two hours before the start.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence should Tully cut?
encounters.success: The paragraph is about Tully's training plan. When the race is held each year isn't part of her plan.

options.text: Then she adds a hill run each Saturday.
options.reason: This belongs. A weekly hill run is part of the plan.

options.text: Tully says the hill runs build the strength she needs for the last climb.
options.reason: This belongs. It says why the hill runs are in her plan.

options.text: The race is held every year in the last week of term.
On race morning, she eats porridge two hours before the start.
options.reason: This belongs. What she eats on race morning is the last step of the plan.

encounters.frame: Wren's science article on coral is nearly ready. Krak has made one cut, and the Strandle wants to know why.
encounters.text: When the ocean stays one or two degrees too warm for weeks, corals push out the tiny algae living inside them. Those algae give coral most of its colour, so without them it turns a ghostly white. They also make most of the coral's food, which means a bleached coral slowly starves. If the water cools in time, the algae can return and the coral may recover. Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor.
encounters.prompt: Krak cut the last sentence. Which reason explains the cut best?
encounters.success: Same subject isn't enough. Every sentence must explain bleaching, and the reef-size fact doesn't.

options.text: It isn't about coral at all, so it has wandered right off the topic.
options.reason: It is about coral. That's what makes it sneaky.

options.text: It's about coral, but every other sentence explains bleaching, and this one doesn't.
It has a number in it, and science articles should explain, not count.
options.reason: The first sentence has numbers too. Numbers are fine when they fit the main idea.

options.text: It comes last, and the last sentence should always sum up the paragraph.
options.reason: Where it sits isn't the problem. It would be cut wherever it went.

encounters.frame: The Redpen Rumble is reporting on the beach's new robot lifeguard. Two editors want to cut different sentences.
encounters.text: The new robot lifeguard at Hollowgum Beach has had a rocky first week. On Monday, it mistook a floating pool noodle for a swimmer and dragged it heroically to shore. Head lifeguard Bev says she laughed so hard she had to sit down on the sand. The robot was built on the mainland and cost the council forty thousand dollars. By Friday, it had blown its whistle at a seagull more than four hundred times.
encounters.prompt: Krak wants to cut Bev's sentence. Gus wants to cut the sentence about the cost. Who is right?
encounters.success: Gus is right. Bev's laugh is about a mistake, so it stays. The cost isn't part of the rocky week.

options.text: Krak, because Bev's sentence is only what someone says, so it can't belong.
options.reason: That shortcut fails. Bev laughing shows how silly the noodle rescue was.

options.text: Both, because neither sentence is one of the robot's actual mistakes.
options.reason: Bev's laugh isn't a mistake, but it shows how silly the noodle rescue was, so it stays.

options.text: Gus, because the cost is about the robot but not about its rocky week.
Neither, because every sentence is about the robot lifeguard, so they all stay.
options.reason: Being about the robot isn't enough. The cost doesn't show a rocky week.

encounters.frame: Indi is writing about her newest mural. The Strandle wants a strand that fits.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong, then choose one that fits.
encounters.success: The paragraph is about thrown-away paint. How long the mural took isn't, but waiting for more thrown-out paint is.

parts.tap: Every drop of paint in Indi's newest mural was paint that someone else had thrown away.

parts.tap: The tins came from the island tip, where people dump half-used paint after fixing up their homes.

parts.reason: This belongs. It tells you how she used the thrown-away paint.

parts.tap: Because the supply was so random, the sky ended up a strange purple-grey.
parts.reason: This belongs. The odd sky colour came from using leftover paint.

parts.tap: Not a single one of her forty-two tins was bought from a shop.
parts.reason: This belongs. It shows none of the paint was new.

options.text: The mural shows the island ferry, the lighthouse and three pelicans.
options.reason: This is about what the mural shows, not the thrown-away paint.

options.text: When one colour ran out, she had to wait for someone to throw out more.
Indi's mural won a prize at the island show last spring.
options.reason: This is about the mural winning a prize, not where the paint came from.

options.text: Indi's favourite paint colour is bright orange, like a sunset.
options.reason: This is about her favourite colour, not paint other people threw away.

encounters.frame: Zed's review of Penguin Panic has two paragraphs: how you play, and what players think. The Strandle is sorting his sentences.
encounters.prompt: Match each sentence to the paragraph it belongs in, or to neither.

items.text: You guide a lost penguin through a maze of melting ice floes.

items.text: Each level gives you sixty seconds before the ice starts to crack.
items.reason: This is a rule of the game, so it goes in paragraph 1.

items.text: The same studio is making a game about lost puffins for next year.
items.reason: This is about a different game. It isn't how you play this one or what players think.

items.text: Some reviewers complain that the music gets annoying after an hour.

items.text: If you fall in, you restart from the last iceberg you touched.
items.reason: This is a rule of the game, so it goes in paragraph 1.

encounters.frame: The Redpen Rumble is running a story about the lava tube ghost tour. The Strandle says to read to the end before you cut.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't belong.
encounters.success: The last sentence gives the main idea: the tour is scary. How the tunnels formed isn't scary at all.

parts.tap: Guides lead groups by torchlight through tunnels so narrow that you must crawl on your hands and knees.
parts.reason: This belongs. Crawling through narrow tunnels in the dark is scary.

parts.tap: Somewhere in the dark, water drips with a sound like slow footsteps.
parts.reason: This belongs. Sounds like footsteps in the dark are spooky.

parts.tap: The tunnels were made thousands of years ago by rivers of lava flowing under the ground.
Halfway through, the guide switches off every torch and tells the tale of a miner whose lantern still flickers in the deepest cave.
parts.reason: This belongs. A ghost story in total darkness is the scariest part.

parts.tap: More than one visitor has begged to be taken back to the entrance.
parts.reason: This belongs. It shows how scared visitors get.

parts.tap: No wonder people say the ghost tour of Redpen Volcano's lava tubes is the scariest trip on the island.
parts.reason: This gives the main idea. Here it comes last instead of first.

encounters.frame: Wren is writing about Maxx Vantablack's latest 'rescue' video. The Strandle wants one strand out.
encounters.text: Maxx Vantablack's latest 'rescue' video was full of mistakes that sharp-eyed fans spotted straight away. The video has already been watched more than nine million times. In one shot, the 'wild' koala he saved was wearing a price tag from a toy shop. Later, the 'stormy sea' behind him was clearly a paddling pool with a leaf blower aimed at it. Worst of all, a crew member's reflection appeared in his sunnies, holding up a sign that said CRY NOW.
encounters.prompt: Wren cut the sentence about nine million views. What does that cut do for her reader?
encounters.success: Every sentence left is a mistake fans spotted, so the reader moves through them without a break.

options.text: It lets the reader go from one mistake to the next without wandering off.
It stops the reader from finding out that Maxx made any mistakes at all.
options.reason: The mistakes are all still there. Only the views sentence went.

options.text: It tells the reader that the video wasn't very popular after all.
options.reason: Cutting a sentence doesn't make it untrue. It just keeps the paragraph on the mistakes.

options.text: It leaves the reader without the strongest proof that the video was faked.
options.reason: Views don't prove anything about faking. The price tag, the pool and the reflection do.
